title: Hosted API demo — chat & text generation basics
summary: Intro demo of Redwood Hosted API focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming, key parameters, retry behavior, and security considerations. Customer interested in a short POC and security docs before committing to Dedicated.

Share security docs (SOC2, ISO) and KMS integration guide
Run a 1-week pilot with 10k requests/day - Arjun to scope

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-24
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 38 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Verdant), Darius Cole (Verdant), Priya Singh (Verdant)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I see we' ve got most folks here, awesome. Quick agenda: i' ll run through the Hosted API chat/text basics, Arjun will demo streaming and some param tuning, and we' ll leave time for security questions.

[00:22] Lena Ortiz: Thanks Maya. Quick intro — I'm Lena, head of ML at Verdant. We're evaluating hosted options for customer-facing summarization and a chat assistant. Main concerns are latency and cost, plus security.

[00:36] Maya Chen: Great, that's exactly what we'll cover. Arjun, want to jump into the demo?

[00:40] Arjun Patel: Yeah, sure. I'll share my screen — hope you can see the console. (screen share noise) Okay, so first high level: our Hosted API supports chat, text generation, embeddings. For chat here, you can stream tokens back over the websocket/HTTP stream, or do single-shot responses. Streaming helps with perceived latency for users.

[01:05] Darius Cole: Sorry quick Q — does streaming require a specific SDK or can we do it with plain HTTP?

[01:10] Arjun Patel: Good question. You can use our SDKs (node/python) which wire up streams for you, but the HTTP endpoint supports chunked transfer encoding too. We also expose a simple event stream that is SSE-compatible. So, both options.

[01:30] Arjun Patel: I'll show a quick curl example of a streaming call. (typing) So you see we open connection, we get partial tokens as they generate, and then a final done event. This is useful if your UI wants to render tokens as they arrive.

[01:50] Lena Ortiz: Do partial tokens include likelihoods / probabilities? We need to do re-ranking client-side.

[01:55] Arjun Patel: We return token text and metadata. For privacy we don't return raw logits by default but we can include score approximations on request. There is a flag in the API params for 'return_token_scores' — it adds some overhead but available.

[02:15] Maya Chen: Also worth noting we have server-side reranking integration if you want to avoid client-side heavy lifting — can surface best N candidates.

[02:30] Darius Cole: Nice. On params — what are the knobs we should tune for latency vs quality?

[02:35] Arjun Patel: Mostly temperature, top_p, max_tokens, and frequency/penalty values. For latency, max_tokens and the model choice are the biggest levers. A lower temperature reduces hallucination variance but doesn't necessarily speed up token generation. Also streaming reduces time-to-first-byte.

[02:55] Arjun Patel: Here's an example request body: model: "redwood-chat-1", temperature: 0.2, top_p: 0.9, max_tokens: 256, stream: true. You can also set 'stop' tokens.

[03:15] Lena Ortiz: We have bursty traffic — mornings with big batch of queries. How does your rate limiting and retry policy work?

[03:22] Maya Chen: By default there's a per-account token quota and per-second QPS limits. We expose headers in responses to show remaining quota. For bursts, we recommend either Dedicated capacity or the hosted with burst allowance — we can configure burst windows.

[03:40] Arjun Patel: On retries: our client SDK implements exponential backoff with jitter. For idempotent requests (like embeddings or stateless generation with a request id), the SDK retries automatically on 5xx or transient network errors. For streaming requests, retries re-establish the stream and resume if you pass a cache key / conversation id — otherwise you might re-run generation.

[04:05] Priya Singh: Pause — on retries and logs, do you persist prompts or responses in your logs? We need to ensure PII isn't stored in plaintext.

[04:12] Maya Chen: By default hosted logs retain a short audit trail for troubleshooting — prompts can be scrubbed. For customers with stricter requirements we recommend Private deployment or Dedicated with log redaction. We have KMS integration for encrypting at rest and options for not storing request payloads. We'll send the detailed security doc.

[04:35] Arjun Patel: Back to streaming demo — you may see minor transcript errors in the auto-capture, e.g., 'K V cache' turned up as 'kinda cache' in earlier recordings — our transcription isn't the focus here but wanted to note.

[04:52] Arjun Patel: I'm going to run two calls side-by-side: one with temperature 0.9 and one with 0.2. Watch the outputs. (typing, brief pause) You can see higher temp gives more varied phrasing, and lower temp is more conservative.

[05:15] Darius Cole: For cost calc, do you charge by prompt tokens + completion tokens? And is streaming any different?

[05:22] Maya Chen: Correct — pricing is per token (prompt + completion). Streaming doesn't change unit costs — it's just delivery. We also show per-request token breakdown in the Console so you can attribute spend to features.

[05:40] Lena Ortiz: Any guidance on batching and KV cache? We're doing a lot of short prompts, can batching help?

[05:48] Arjun Patel: Yes, our runtime does continuous batching under the hood for hosted. If you send many short messages concurrently, the runtime will batch them to GPUs to improve throughput. For chat with long contexts, the KV cache helps for repeated system messages or long conversation prefixes — avoids recomputing those parts.

[06:10] Maya Chen: Also Redwood Optimize will suggest batching configs and quantization profiles if you run a workload through our optimizer, can reduce unit cost significantly.

[06:25] Lena Ortiz: We heard about quantized models — are those available on hosted? Tradeoffs?

[06:30] Arjun Patel: We host curated quantized variants that are Redwood-verified. They reduce memory and cost but can have small quality delta on some prompts. Our Optimize tool recommends which quantization profiles to use per workload.

[06:50] Darius Cole: Back to retries — what's the typical SLO on 1XX/5XX errors and how does fallback to compatible models work?

[06:58] Arjun Patel: For hosted we aim for 99.9% availability for standard tiers. If a model variant is under pressure, we can auto-fallback to a compatible variant (e.g., quantized variant) or to a lower-tier model to preserve latency. Fallback is configurable per-route.

[07:20] Priya Singh: On compliance — do you have SOC 2 and iso? And can we get an audit report?

[07:25] Maya Chen: Yes SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001. We'll attach the compliance pack and an NDA if needed for the audit artifacts.

[07:35] Arjun Patel: I'm going to show an SDK retry snippet — here we set maxRetries: 4, backoffFactor: 2, jitter: true. For idempotency we recommend a client-supplied request_id.

[07:50] Lena Ortiz: For our streaming UI we need to render partials and also support mid-stream cancellation — can we cancel a stream and be billed only for tokens generated up to that point?

[07:59] Arjun Patel: Yes, cancellation is supported. Billing is based on tokens generated before cancellation. If you cancel mid-token because of transport issues, the token count rounds to the last completed token.

[08:20] Darius Cole: What about rate limiting headers? Can we programmatically detect throttling?

[08:25] Arjun Patel: We include X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, Retry-After when throttled. SDK surfaces these to help you decide to backoff.

[08:40] Maya Chen: Quick product note: Console has per-route dashboards where you can see latency P50/P95/P99 and token spend, and set alerts.

[08:50] Lena Ortiz: Can you show how to set up a conversation state with the SDK — maintain context across requests?

[08:56] Arjun Patel: Sure. Example: you send prior messages array with role:user/system/assistant. We also support a conversation_id param so the runtime can do prefix caching and speed up subsequent calls if you re-use prefixes.

[09:20] Arjun Patel: (demo continues) Now I'm simulating bursty load — watch how the runtime batches and you see throughput increase. The console chart updates with requests/sec.

[09:45] Darius Cole: Nice. For a POC, what do you recommend we test? Latency at 99th pct, cost per 1k completions, and hallucination regression on our prompt set?

[09:55] Maya Chen: Exactly. Typical POC scope: ingest a sample prompt set, run A/B across model variants, measure P95 latency, cost, and quality (via evals). Arjun will help with scripts.

[10:10] Lena Ortiz: Can you do retention controls? We can't have prompts stored for our customers in raw form.

[10:16] Maya Chen: Yes we offer request data retention controls and log redaction. For the hosted tier we can enable no-persist mode for sensitive routes — though some features like long-term observability will be limited unless you accept retention. Dedicated/Private gives full control.

[10:35] Priya Singh: If we go hosted with no-persist, do you still have ephemeral caching that could surface data to other tenants?

[10:42] Arjun Patel: No, caches are per-tenant. KV cache is scoped to the tenant's model instance. For strict isolation we recommend Dedicated.

[11:00] Maya Chen: Quick recap of model selection: we recommend running both a fast quantized variant and a high-quality float variant in parallel for canary testing. Use auto-fallback to keep latency SLOs.

[11:20] Arjun Patel: One more demo: showing how retries + idempotency works in a script. (typing noises) If a 502 happens, SDK retries up to N times; if you provide request_id it will avoid double-processing for side-effectful calls.

[11:45] Darius Cole: Good. On enterprise terms: what's included in Hosted vs Dedicated pricing?

[11:52] Maya Chen: Hosted is usage-based with per-token pricing and optional add-ons for longer retention and SLAs. Dedicated is reserved capacity (monthly commit) with predictable throughput, stricter isolation, and extended SLAs. We'll send a pricing comparison.

[12:10] Lena Ortiz: Can you run a short benchmark for us — focus on 99th percentile latency for our typical prompt length (avg 120 tokens)?

[12:17] Arjun Patel: Yep, Arjun: I'll scope a benchmark plan in the next 48 hours. We'll need a small sample prompt set and target QPS.

[12:30] Priya Singh: Also need details on KMS integration and key rotation.

[12:34] Maya Chen: We'll include KMS/HSM integration docs in the security pack.

[12:42] Lena Ortiz: Timeline wise — we want to decide by mid-September. How fast can a POC be started?

[12:48] Maya Chen: We can kick off a hosted POC within a couple of days pending paperwork. Dedicated takes longer. We'll aim to have POC scripts and pricing by Friday.

[13:00] Arjun Patel: Closing demo — any other technical questions?

[13:05] Darius Cole: One last one — in case of model fallback, do you get a header or event indicating fallback happened so we can log it?

[13:12] Arjun Patel: Yes we'll include X-Fallback-Model and a reason code in response headers when fallback occurs. Useful for tracking.

[13:25] Priya Singh: Ok that helps.

[13:30] Maya Chen: Great, quick recap of action items and next steps: we' ll send pricing and security docs, Arjun will scope the POC and provide scripts, Verdant to share prompt set and SLOs. I'll follow up with a calendar invite for the POC kickoff the week of Aug 31.

[13:50] Lena Ortiz: Thanks, appreciate the demo — we'll look out for the docs.

[13:55] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, talk soon.

(Transcript notes: transcription imperfect — some technical terms like 'KV cache' may be slightly garbled in the auto text.)
